sweep_summary: Papiamento (papi1253) is in the catalog as 'lexical' on Remijsen & van Heuven 2005. the list of works with stress in the title holds three distinct works (seven Glottolog records, all already listed). (1) Remijsen & van Heuven 2005: downloaded the open Leiden postprint (hdl:1887/14092) and read §2.2.1-2.2.3; the catalog quote is verbatim from p. 207 and the paper states stress is lexically distinctive (disyllabic verb base penult vs participle final; non-verbs weight-sensitive penult/final with many irregular final/penult/antepenult exceptions) — confirms. new_statements.rule_in_words: Papiamentu has two level tones H and L alongside stress. The authors argue (p. 12) that 'with few exceptions, the placement of H and main stress in Papiamentu words can be predicted from categorial class membership and syllable weight'. Verbs: stress depends on syllable count - bisyllabic verbs always have penultimate (initial) stress with H on the final syllable (H and stress do not coincide, e.g. kaska 'peel', mata 'kill'); trisyllabic and longer verbs have final H and final stress (kuminsá 'begin'); monosyllabic verbs trivially final. Nouns, adjectives, adverbs: weight-sensitive - final H and stress if the final syllable is heavy (rhyme with at least two weight units, e.g. falis 'suitcase', karèt 'currant'), penultimate H and stress if the final syllable is light (buraku 'hole'). Words ending in l,r,n after schwa (òrgel, sténdert) count as light because the final rhyme is a syllabic sonorant. Participles of bisyllabic verbs shift H and stress to the final syllable (fadá 'tired'). Roughly 250 bisyllabic minimal pairs differ by tone melody alone (HL vs LH) with the same penultimate stress (papa 'porridge' vs papa 'father'). Phonetic correlates: loudness plus optional lengthening on L-toned stressed syllables of bisyllabic verbs; loudness plus high pitch in longer verbs.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Secondary stress is assigned to alternating syllables; we will not discuss it.' (p. 13). In longer verbs 'We either find L on all preceding syllables, or alternating HL: speakers which have the latter pattern realise secondary stress as H.' (p. 13). Per Römer (1991: 47) some speakers have (L)HLL on irregular-antepenult words, others (L)HLH, 'secondary stress - which is assigned to alternating syllables - is realised by the latter class of speakers as H' (p. 14).
new_statements.exceptions: p. 14: 'Genuine exceptions are of the following kinds: (i) words with H and stress on the wrong syllable, i.e. either on a final light syllable, or on an (ante)penultimate syllable where the final syllable is heavy; (ii) words in which the placement of H is irregular.' Examples (7): irregular final stress karnisá 'pickled meat', mashá 'very', muhé 'woman'; antepenultimate ásido 'acid', rápido 'fast', idéntiko 'identical'; penultimate difísil 'difficult', mártir 'martyr'; (8) irregular melody ónzebar 'poltergeist', mucha 'child', tambe 'too, also'. Bisyllabic verbs with irregular HL melody (4): sunchi, skeiru, feter, beitel, wèlder, freta, fangu (all Dutch or English origin). Inherited compounds (bistek, failkast) have H on adjacent syllables (§1.3.6). Nouns formed with autostressed -dó and with -mentu retain base stress; adjectives in -bel have penultimate stress. Noun/verb pairs differ by tone shift or stress shift (§2.5.1.2-4).
new_statements.identity_note: Kouwenberg & Murray 1994 describe Papiamentu of all three ABC islands, not the Curaçao dialect alone: they adopt Curaçaoan spelling ('We have adopted the Curaçaon spelling for this description of Papiamentu, except where in chapter 4 examples are quoted from Aruban sources', p. 4), state that 'There are some dialectal differences among the three islands, but the dialects are mutually [intelligible]' (p. 4-5), and used native-speaker consultants from both Curaçao and Aruba (p. 5). Their tone facts are drawn largely from Römer (1977, 1991) and Dijkhoff (1993), i.e. Curaçao-based work, so the stress description is compatible with the catalog's Curaçao Papiamentu entry (Glottolog papi1253 covers Papiamento as a whole).

new_statements.quote: Treatments of Papiamentu stress have assumed it to follow an Iberian pattern, and the orthography reflects this. Regular stress is thought to be penultimate for words ending in a vowel or l,r,n, final for words ending in another consonant or a diphthong. In words that do not conform to this pattern the placement of stress is marked in the orthography by an acute. This creates an immediate problem for the treatment of verbs: all trisyllabic and longer verbs end in a vowel and have final stress. These are thus treated as an open-ended class of exceptions, although their behaviour is fully predictable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Papiamentu is described as a mixed system with 'fully functional stress and tonal systems' of 'equal status': every word has exactly one primary stress, placed by default on the penult, but stress position is lexically/morphologically distinctive (minimal triplet 'matá 'to kill' / ma'tá 'killed' / 'máta 'plant'; 'piska verb vs pis'ka noun). Table 1 (after Kouwenberg & Murray 1994, Maurer 1998): disyllabic verbs penult stress + final H; past participles final stress + H; polysyllabic words final stress + H with weak stress on the antepenult; nouns with a heavy final syllable (or deverbal nouns) final stress; nouns with a light final syllable penult stress + H; a penult H tone attracts stress. Phonetically, stress is cued by duration (stressed syllables about twice as long as unstressed ones in the same position), tone by F0.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary ('weak') stress in polysyllabic words, e.g. "kumin'sá 'begun' with secondary on the initial/antepenult; an unstressed syllable is required between primary and secondary stress (rhythmic alternation); only one primary stress per word.
new_statements.exceptions: Past participles take final stress 'except for those ending in L tone or monosyllabic forms with a prefix e-'; nouns with a heavy final syllable and nouns derived from verbs take final stress (ru'mán); some adjectives and nouns combine H tone and stress on the penult (a'mígu, 'máta, 'hómber, pu'síbel); 'There are exceptions to these patterns, but most members of these categories conform'; stress shifts to the penult of the complex when an H-tone pronoun encliticises to a verb ('yuda + ábo -> yu'dábu); citation forms further conditioned by phrase-level tone (contours phrase-internally, floating H utterance-finally); sentence-final lengthening can make a final unstressed syllable as long as a preceding stressed one.
new_statements.identity_note: Rivera-Castillo & Pickering's instrumental data come from a single Aruban speaker (keywords include 'Aruba'; ex. (10) 'a typical Aruban house'), i.e. Aruban Papiamento rather than the Curaçao dialect named in the catalog record; their phonological description, however, is pan-Papiamentu and drawn from Curaçao-based sources (Harris 1951, Römer 1980-1991, Kouwenberg & Murray 1994, Maurer 1998). Glottolog papi1253 covers Papiamento as a whole (Aruba, Bonaire, Curaçao).

tone_statements.quote: Römer (1992) describes tonal phenomena in Papiamento. We find level high and low tones, which in many - but by no means all - cases correspond to accented and unaccented syllables, repsectively. A major class of exceptions is formed by the bisyllabic verbs. These have a Low High pattern with the Low tone realised on the accented syllable, as in 'pone ‘to put’, 'kwèrdè ‘to wind’, 'laba ‘wash’. There are minimal pairs such as papa ‘porridge; the Pope’ with a High Low pattern, and papa ‘dad’ with a Low High tonal pattern (Römer 1992).

tone_statements.quote: The Iberian-lexifier creole Papiamentu, spoken in the Netherlands Antilles, combines stress from its European heritage with tone (and various tonal processes) from its African lineage (Rivera-Castillo & Pickering 2004). The vowels of stressed syllables are longer and louder than unstressed ones, and unstressed syllables tend to be more centralized (i.e. more schwa-like) than stressed ones (Remijsen & van Heuven 2005:223). At the same time, syllables marked for H and for L differ consistently in pitch in a way similar to that established for CAF and EGS (see §3.5). [p. 25]

sources.note: Curaçao Papiamentu has lexically distinctive stress and, independently, a privative word-level tone contrast. Verbs: disyllabic base = penult stress, participle = final stress (mata/matá), 3+ syllables final in both. Non-verbs: weight-sensitive (penult unless final syllable closed), with many lexifier-inherited exceptions (final, penult, antepenult: 'hoben, li'he, 'aguila). Secondary stress on alternating syllables. §2.2.3: 'Stress is distinctive in most disyllabic verbs, where it distinguishes the base form from the participle.' tone.quote: Both stress and tone are to some extent unpredictable and therefore distinctive in Curaçao Papiamentu. Stress is distinctive in most disyllabic verbs, where it distinguishes the base form from the participle. Tone distinguishes disyllabic verbs (tone II) from disyllabic non-verbs (tone I). [p. 210] ... the vowels of stressed syllables in Curaçao Papiamentu have a greater duration and greater intensity, and are more peripheral in the vowel space. Interestingly, this stress prominence is lexically distinctive, independent of the lexical tone contrast. [p. 225] ... the final syllable of words with antepenultimate stress has secondary stress rather than a tonal specification. [p. 226]

sources.quote: Treatments of Papiamentu stress have assumed it to follow an Iberian pattern, and the orthography reflects this. Regular stress is thought to be penultimate for words ending in a vowel or l,r,n, final for words ending in another consonant or a diphthong. In words that do not conform to this pattern the placement of stress is marked in the orthography by an acute. This creates an immediate problem for the treatment of verbs: all trisyllabic and longer verbs end in a vowel and have final stress. These are thus treated as an open-ended class of exceptions, although their behaviour is fully predictable.
sources.note: Same work as index 0; see that entry. The quoted p. 13 passage also documents the older Iberian-style description of Papiamentu stress (penult after vowel/l,r,n, final otherwise, acute marks exceptions), which the authors reject for verbs.

sources.quote: The Iberian-lexifier creole Papiamentu, spoken in the Netherlands Antilles, combines stress from its European heritage with tone (and various tonal processes) from its African lineage (Rivera-Castillo & Pickering 2004). The vowels of stressed syllables are longer and louder than unstressed ones, and unstressed syllables tend to be more centralized (i.e. more schwa-like) than stressed ones (Remijsen & van Heuven 2005:223). At the same time, syllables marked for H and for L differ consistently in pitch in a way similar to that established for CAF and EGS (see §3.5). [p. 25]

sources.quote: Römer (1992) describes tonal phenomena in Papiamento. We find level high and low tones, which in many - but by no means all - cases correspond to accented and unaccented syllables, repsectively. A major class of exceptions is formed by the bisyllabic verbs. These have a Low High pattern with the Low tone realised on the accented syllable, as in 'pone ‘to put’, 'kwèrdè ‘to wind’, 'laba ‘wash’. There are minimal pairs such as papa ‘porridge; the Pope’ with a High Low pattern, and papa ‘dad’ with a Low High tonal pattern (Römer 1992).
sources.note: Level High and Low tones (after Römer 1992) beside penult/final word stress; tone only partly matches stress: bisyllabic verbs Low-High with Low on stressed syllable, nouns High-Low; 251 tonal pairs.
